name: Electric corset

card.summary: A Victorian-era corset sold with magnets or electric elements, marketed to shape the figure and improve health and comfort.
card.aka: Dr. Scott's Electric Corset; Harness' Electropathic corset
card.note: Historical product; contemporary critics and courts disputed its health claims.

quick.overview:
The electric corset was a late nineteenth-century corset marketed with claims of electricity or magnetism. Dr. Scott's Electric Corset was an American invention sold in Britain by the Pall Mall Electric Association, and C. B. Harness sold his own version from about 1891.

The appearance payoff was the normal corset effect, a shaped waist and figure, with advertising adding promised health and vitality benefits. Reports state that the 'electric' feature in Harness's version was a magnetised steel busk.
quick.how: Wearers put it on like an ordinary corset, and advertising promised comfort, beauty and health. Products were sold by mail and through newspaper advertisements.
quick.risks: Corsets in general can reduce lung capacity and are linked to muscle and organ effects with tight lacing. Harness's company faced lawsuits and a fraud prosecution over its electropathic products.

lead: Electric corsets were corsets sold in the 1880s and 1890s with claims that built-in electricity or magnetism improved health while shaping the figure. Dr. Scott's Electric Corset came from the American inventor George A. Scott, whose Pall Mall Electric Association also sold electric brushes.[1]

One Wellcome Collection pamphlet from the Pall Mall Electric Association on the corset is catalogued as about 1882, and 1886 New Zealand newspaper advertisements pitched it for health, comfort and beauty.[1]

Cornelius Bennett Harness first distributed Scott's corset, then sold his own version from 1891, reported to be magnetic rather than electric, with a magnetised steel busk as its only special feature.[1]

chain: Visible waist reduction and posture support
angle.text: As a corset it shapes the waist and torso. The electric or magnetic feature was marketed for health, and no evidence for it is recorded.

paras: Scott became known in London and New York from about 1878 for advertising electric brushes, and his association also sold an electric corset and an electropathic belt for ladies. Harness ran the Medical Battery Company, whose main product was an electropathic belt with zinc and copper plates.[1]

The Pall Mall Gazette ran a flattering piece in August 1892 that was in fact advertising, then in 1893 dropped the company's ads and published an exposé; the Electrical Review described the firm's activities as grossly misrepresented.[1] In 1892 a customer who refused to pay for a belt won a case, and in November 1893 Harness and a colleague were charged with conspiracy to defraud; the jury could not agree on Harness, and the company was wound up.[1] Harness died in 1921.[1]
Corsets in general can reduce lung capacity (an average of about 9 percent for moderate lacing), and long-term use may contribute to core muscle wasting; findings on skeletal effects are mixed.[2]

timeline.event: George A. Scott becomes known for advertising electric brushes.
Harness sells his own electric corset from Oxford Street.[1]
